newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Socialists search for Gonzalez successor.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Socialists search for Gonzalez successor.

text.p: Spain's Socialists scrambled to find a new leader on Saturday, narrowing the field of top candidates after former Prime Minister Felipe Gonzalez announced he would not run again as party chief.

With little more than 24 hours left to come up with a replacement, no clear frontrunner had emerged, but senior party officials were giving strong consideration to a list of about half a dozen names, insiders said.

Gonzalez, who led his party away from Marxism and through 13 years in government, dropped a bombshell at the opening of the Socialist Workers' Party congress on Friday when he told delegates it was time for a "change of generations." "Please replace me," he urged.

The 55-year-old Gonzalez, who has shown signs of wearying of political life since Spanish voters pushed him out of office last year, has dominated his party like few other Western European politicians.
But so far, he has given no hint of his choice for a successor to take the Socialists into the next general election scheduled for the year 2000.
Caught off guard by Gonzalez' announcement, the party's executive committee worked through the night in an effort to reach consensus on a final list of candidates.
They have until Sunday -- the last day of the congress -- to present their recommendations to a vote by the party's 1,000 delegates, who will decide on the next secretary-general.

Not a single Socialist leader has yet stepped forward and publicly declared his candidacy -- Spanish politicians usually handle such matters behind closed doors. And party members said the race was still wide open.
Joaquin Almunia, the party's high-profile parliamentary spokesman, was one name most frequently mentioned by delegates, but he would not say whether he was interested in the job.
"Talk of me running as secretary-general has no foundation and no credibility as it is very early on in the congress," Almunia told reporters.

Other candidates include regional leaders Jose Bono of Castilla-La Mancha and Manuel Chaves of Andalusia and Basque socialist chief Ramon Jauregui, but some delegates believe they lack the national profile needed to run the party.
The Socialists' former government spokesman, Alfredo Perez Rubalcaba, and parliamentary deputy Jose Borrell, an ex-minister, were also under consideration.
But the clear favorite of the party's rank-and-file, NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, has already taken himself out of the running.

A party official said Solana, a former Socialist foreign minister, wants to see NATO through the first stage of its planned eastward expansion but might be ready to return to Spanish politics after his term ends in 1999.

One day after Gonzalez's surprise announcement, the party faithful were still reeling from the impact. "We've only just started thinking about Socialism without Felipe. It's been such a shock," said Maria Antonia Armengol, a member of the executive committee.

But Socialist insiders mostly agreed that Gonzalez' departure was needed to begin a major overhaul of the party, which was left demoralized by its defeat by the centre-right Popular Party led by Jose Maria Aznar.

The Socialist-leaning daily El Pais praised Gonzalez for relinquishing power, saying it shows he is "a politican of the highest quality of his generation and that he understands it's time to give way to the next."
But the centre-right El Mundo newspaper suggested it was merely a "strategic withdrawal" that would allow him to keep control behind the scenes and eventually stage a comeback.
Gonzalez swept to power in 1982 on a surge of popular support to rebuild Spain after nearly 40 years of dictatorial rule under General Francisco Franco.

Spanish voters returned him to office three times, but a recent succession of corruption scandals eroded public confidence in Gonzalez and the Socialist leadership and contributed to their defeat last year.
